macro.topic: Why US stocks aren't falling even as bond yields rise

views.view: He said the US 10-year yield passing 5.1% (highest since 2006) hasn't stopped stocks from rising because the market treats AI as immune to macro swings and 'too big to fail,' and that markets can stay irrational for a long time.
views.quote: The market can remain irrational for a long time; instead of denying it, we should go along with what the market is doing.

views.view: He argued mega-cap tech firms (Alphabet, Meta, Oracle) have become as powerful and creditworthy as governments, that their bond issuance (including Alphabet's 100-year 6.125% sterling bond) proves this structural shift, and that it forces Treasury yields to stay high via supply and demand.
views.quote: Treasury yields have been pegged to a new standard. They need to stay high to compete.

views.view: He wrote that the sharp rise in the MOVE index is normally a negative signal for tech stocks, but strong AI-company earnings are currently offsetting the rate pressure, and that his own risk system watches whether SPX and especially NDX sit above or below the 50-day EMA.

persons.name: Bora Özkent
persons.digest:
Bora Özkent lays out four basic ways to make money: labor (selling your time), capital (putting money to work through investing), arbitrage (buying cheap and selling dear — including the information arbitrage he practices himself), and insurance (taking on someone else's risk for a premium). He notes labor has a hard ceiling of about 2,000 working hours a year, making it risky to rely on alone, while a steady $500/month invested in US stocks could grow to $1.13 million over 30 years at a 10% nominal return. He explains information arbitrage through his own business: he gathers data from paid subscriptions, summarizes and adds commentary with AI, then resells it at a higher price to his School members and on social media.

He frames the fourth mechanism, insurance, more broadly than just insurance companies — as guaranteeing a customer outcome or helping reduce someone's risk (such as through stock analysis). He says none of these is enough on its own; for durable, scalable income they must be turned into a system, like his own Terminal platform. He assigns viewers homework: map their own income sources onto these four categories and work out how to turn them into a system.

items.title: There Are 4 Ways to Make Money, the Rest Is Nonsense!
items.summary: Inspired by a tweet, Bora Özkent walks through four mechanisms for making money: labor (selling your time, capped at roughly 2,000 hours a year), capital (regular stock investing — $500/month could grow to $1.13 million over 30 years at a 10% nominal return), arbitrage (buying cheap and selling dear, including the information arbitrage he practices himself by summarizing paid sources with AI and reselling to his School members), and insurance (taking on someone else's risk for a premium, or reducing a customer's risk via a guarantee). He adds a fifth layer — tying all of this into a system, like his own Terminal platform — as what makes income durable and scalable. He assigns viewers homework: map their income sources onto these four categories and work out how to systematize them.

He concludes markets can stay irrational for a long time, so the right move is to go along with market moves rather than deny them.

persons.name: Berk Dinçtürk
persons.digest:
Berk Dinçtürk thinks SPK putting roughly 131 funds from 7 fund managers into liquidation is meant to make the fund market safer and more institutional, not to shrink it, and sees this as laying groundwork for big money coming into Turkey. He says Turkey is gaining geopolitical importance via the middle corridor and its defense industry, which will eventually pull in capital, and that companies like **Turkish Airlines**, trading below book value, are a good opportunity for investors especially after the Boeing deal.

On the US side, he explains that even though the Fed unexpectedly hiked rates, the economy is growing at 6.5% nominal, and with $40 trillion in debt the Fed has very little tolerance for recession. He says the **S&P 500**'s PEG ratio is at a 30-year low, sees upside through year-end, but notes the window is narrowing and recommends carrying existing positions with trailing stops. As a new investment theme, he says AI is shifting from hardware to software, making crypto assets and tokenization increasingly important, and recommends a slice of the portfolio in metals/commodities (rare earths, **gold**, **silver**, **copper**). Given the global debt load and central banks diversifying reserves, he expects **gold** to reach 5-digit levels (above $10,000) by the end of the Trump term, with **silver** following the same rally. He adds that the **Korea index**, up 120% before pulling back to a 70% gain, looks overextended and isn't the place to look for new opportunities — pointing instead to commodity-rich South American markets like Brazil and Argentina.

assets.note: Sees a technical breakout; holding his ~11% position while waiting for the Neutron launch.

persons.name: cevikfinance
persons.digest: cevikfinance shared the news that Trump rejected Iran's ceasefire offer, noting he had predicted it; he called the eight-point outcome of the Xi-Trump meeting (reciprocal tariff cut, Iran's non-nuclear commitment, a new AI dialogue, etc.) good news for the market. He wrote that a rising MOVE index is normally bad for tech stocks, but strong AI-company earnings are currently offsetting that pressure, and that his own risk system watches whether SPX/NDX sit above or below the 50-day EMA.

items.title: Trump rejected Iran's ceasefire offer
